query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of hafnium (Hf) to a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with lamellar colony microstructure will improve both room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility by forming fine Hf‐rich precipitates that strengthen the matrix and pin internal boundaries, thereby arresting microcrack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNi-based EHEA with a dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure that exhibits room-temperature brittleness due to internal boundaries acting as microcrack nucleation sites.
generation.intervention: Introduce a slight Hf addition (e.g., targeting an Hf0.5 modified composition) during alloy synthesis and subsequent thermo-mechanical processing.
generation.conditions: Casting, rolling, and annealing conditions that preserve the lamellar colony structure while allowing the formation of fine, uniformly distributed Hf-rich precipitates at grain and phase boundaries at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine Hf-rich precipitates located at the phase and grain boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The Hf-rich precipitates provide dual benefits: (1) precipitation strengthening by impeding dislocation motion and (2) a boundary‐pinning effect that arrests microcrack initiation and propagation along the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies, thereby mitigating premature fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Hf-modified EHEA will exhibit higher yield and tensile strengths as well as an increased tensile ductility at room temperature owing to the combined effects of precipitate strengthening and microcrack arrest.
generation.baseline: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy with its conventional lamellar microstructure, which typically shows high strength but limited ductility due to early microcrack formation along phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective when the processing conditions allow for the formation of a stable, fine dispersion of Hf-rich precipitates; deviations in processing or excessive Hf additions that lead to coarse precipitate formation or deleterious phase transformations may not yield the predicted improvements.
generation.uncertainty: While there is evidence that Hf additions improve high-temperature performance, its effectiveness at room temperature in arresting microcrack propagation in lamellar EHEAs is less established and requires experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys with identical casting, rolling, and annealing processing: one set with the conventional AlCoCrFeNi-based composition and one set with the same composition modified with an Hf addition targeting an Hf0.5 level. Characterize both sets for their microstructures (using TEM/SEM) to confirm precipitate formation at phase boundaries, then perform room-temperature tensile tests to evaluate yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of precipitate size, distribution, and phase boundaries
Room-temperature tensile strength, yield strength, and plastic strain measurements
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the unmodified alloy, or if the precipitate distribution does not correlate with a reduction in microcrack propagation, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
